title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.
why: This asks how much graph information is needed to answer a single matching query while remaining consistent with all other answers. A polynomial degree bound would give a deterministic local oracle for a basic graph primitive with cost independent of graph size. A superpolynomial lower bound would separate this information requirement from the known linear dependence on degree in communication rounds.

importance.reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.

progress.text: As reviewed in the checked 2020 paper, Balliu and coauthors establish the deterministic LOCAL lower bound \(\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})\) for bipartite maximal matching. This yields a degree-linear obstruction for degree-only volume bounds.

Rosenbaum and Suomela formalize connected adaptive volume, and Brandt and Olivetti refine degree-dependent bipartite matching bounds in the round model. Their exact round constants are not asserted as exact volume constants.
Suomela’s updated list retains the explicit polynomial-in-degree volume question and states an exponential-degree conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Suomela’s problem list, updated 23 February 2026, explicitly asks whether maximal matching in bipartite graphs admits volume polynomial in the maximum degree. The supplied coloring and deterministic connected exploration are part of the model used here.

The list records a degree-only lower bound \(\Omega(\Delta)\) and an upper bound \((\Delta+1)^{O(\Delta)}\) for volume. These bounds leave open whether some fixed polynomial in \(\Delta\) is sufficient.

Rosenbaum and Suomela define volume by the number of distinct vertices seen through adaptive connected queries. This can differ substantially from the largest graph distance reached. The output of every rooted execution must still fit the same globally valid solution.
Suomela conjectures a \(2^{\Theta(\Delta)}\) dependence. This is a conjecture about the full degree dependence, and the cited page does not present it as a proved superpolynomial lower bound.
The degree parameter grows in this question. A bound that is constant in graph size for each separately fixed degree does not necessarily give one universal polynomial in the degree.

sentences: A maximal matching is a collection of disjoint edges to which no additional edge can be added.
A vertex query may inspect the graph only by following ports from vertices it has already visited.
The input supplies the two sides of the bipartite graph, and separate queries must describe one consistent matching.
The question asks for one deterministic algorithm whose visited volume is polynomial in the degree bound and independent of graph size.
The February 2026 primary list retains this question between known linear and superpolynomial degree-dependent bounds.
